passage:
Class 5 note, Thursday. Imran, class teacher.
During our lesson on families, Bidisha put her hand up and asked, 'Why do grown-ups say "Respect your elders" every time they're losing an argument?' A few children laughed. She went red but didn't take the question back. After class she told me her Ma says it whenever she asks why she can't go to the park with friends. I explained that respect means being polite and caring, like not shouting and helping an elder carry things, not being scared or never asking questions. She asked if she could still say 'I don't agree' nicely. I said yes, and we practised it once. I will mention our talk to her Ma at the parent meeting.

qa.q: What did Bidisha practise with Imran?
qa.a: Saying 'I don't agree' nicely.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when a few children laughed at her question?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, going red, but also determined, since she didn't take the question back.

qa.q: What did Imran's explanation give Bidisha?
qa.a: A clear meaning of respect as courtesy and care rather than fear, plus a polite way to disagree, so she can keep her manners and her voice.

qa.q: How might Bidisha's Ma see things after hearing about this at the parent meeting?
qa.a: Her Ma might realise that 'respect your elders' leaves Bidisha feeling shut down, and try giving real reasons about the park instead.

grounding: Illustrates a child who is told to respect elders whenever adults disagree, and a teacher who explains respect as courtesy and care rather than fear.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today Dadi switched off my cartoon halfway because it was time for her serial, even though I asked first. When I said that wasn't fair, Papa said, 'Respect your elders, Aparna,' and that was the end of it. Why? Being older doesn't make you right about the TV! I went to my room and cried into the pillow so nobody would hear.
Later Madhav Bhaiya came in. He said respect isn't being scared of Dadi, it's being kind to her, like when I oil her hair on Sundays. He said I can still tell her 'I asked first' in a nice voice. Tomorrow I'll try. Maybe we can take turns.
Aparna, age 10

qa.q: What does Aparna do for Dadi on Sundays?
qa.a: Aparna oils Dadi's hair on Sundays.

qa.q: Why did Aparna cry into the pillow, and what was Aparna feeling?
qa.a: Aparna felt hurt and unheard, because Papa ended the argument with 'respect your elders' instead of a reason.

qa.q: How did Madhav Bhaiya's explanation help Aparna?
qa.a: It showed respect as kindness rather than fear and gave Aparna a polite way to speak up, so Aparna can keep good manners and still have a voice.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel if Aparna says 'I asked first' nicely and offers to take turns?
qa.a: Dadi may feel respected rather than challenged, and could be glad to share the TV.

grounding: Shows a child told to respect elders without any reason when adults disagree, and an older sibling explaining respect as care, not fear, so the child keeps both manners and a voice.

passage:
In the village near Sangrur, Jasleen had a question every day, and every day she got the same answer.

"Why can't I sit on Bapuji's charpai?" Respect your elders.

"Why does Taya-ji get the first roti even when I'm hungrier?" Respect your elders.

"Why can't I say Taya-ji's story is wrong when it IS wrong?" Respect your elders!

On Sunday, Tejas Mama found her sulking by the tubewell. She told him the whole list.

He sat on the cement edge. "Respect isn't being scared, Jasleen. It's being kind in how you speak. You can say, 'Taya-ji, I read it differently,' softly, after dinner. That's respect and your own voice together."

Jasleen tried it that night. Taya-ji raised his eyebrows. Then he said, "Hm. Show me the book."

qa.q: Where did Tejas Mama find Jasleen sulking?
qa.a: Tejas Mama found her sulking by the tubewell.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel hearing 'respect your elders' every day?
qa.a: Jasleen felt frustrated and unheard, because nobody explained why, even when she was sure Taya-ji's story was wrong.

qa.q: What did Tejas Mama's explanation give Jasleen?
qa.a: A reason and a way: respect as kindness in how you speak, so she could disagree softly and keep both her manners and her voice.

qa.q: How might Taya-ji have felt when Jasleen spoke softly after dinner?
qa.a: Taya-ji seemed surprised but open, since he raised his eyebrows and then asked to see the book.

grounding: Shows a child told to respect elders without reasons, and an adult explaining that respect means courtesy, not fear, so she keeps her voice.

passage:
"Girls don't whistle," Dede said, tapping the table in the Istanbul flat.

"Why not?" asked Elif, nine.

"Elif. Respect your elders," said Anne, without looking up from the tea.

It was the third time that week. Elif went to her room and whistled into her pillow.

On Monday she asked her after-school tutor, Dalia, what respect actually meant.

Dalia thought about it. "Respect is being polite and kind. It isn't being afraid. You can respect your Dede and still ask him things, gently, when he's not upset."

That evening Elif brought Dede his tea and sat beside him. "Dede, why don't girls whistle? I really want to know."

He laughed, surprised. "My mother said it scared away luck. Probably nonsense." Then he whistled a tune from his village and taught her the first line.

qa.q: What did Dede say about girls?
qa.a: Dede said, "Girls don't whistle."

qa.q: How did Elif feel when Anne told her to respect her elders?
qa.a: Elif felt frustrated and brushed off, since it was the third time that week and no one explained why.

qa.q: What made Elif's second question to Dede work?
qa.a: She asked gently at a calm moment, after bringing his tea, showing care while still using her own voice.

qa.q: How might Dede see Elif's question the second time?
qa.a: Dede seems pleased and surprised to be asked kindly, enough to share the old saying and teach her a tune.

grounding: Shows a child hushed with 'respect your elders' and then helped to see respect as courtesy and care, so she can ask her question kindly.

passage:
"Respect your seniors, Parul," said the Class 8 prefect, and wrote her name in the late book again, though the gate had opened five minutes late.

Parul, eleven, stamped into Class 6C. "Everyone says respect, respect. Nobody says why."

Nazia ma'am, the class teacher, heard her. At break she called Parul to her desk. "Tell me what happened."

Parul told her about the gate.

"Respect is being polite and fair to people," ma'am said. "It doesn't mean you must accept something unfair. You can be polite and still say, 'The gate opened late; can you check?' Shall we practise?"

They practised twice. At lunch Parul went to the prefect, hands steady. The prefect checked with the guard and crossed out her name.

qa.q: How late did the gate open?
qa.a: The gate had opened five minutes late.

qa.q: Why did Parul stamp into class?
qa.a: Parul was angry and frustrated at being told to respect her seniors while a rule was used unfairly against her.

qa.q: How did Nazia ma'am support Parul?
qa.a: She listened, explained that respect is being polite and fair, not accepting unfairness, and practised polite words with her.

qa.q: How might the prefect see Parul's polite question?
qa.a: The prefect could accept it without feeling challenged, which made it easy to check with the guard and fix it.

grounding: Shows a child told to respect seniors without reasons, and a teacher explaining respect as courtesy so she can speak up politely.

passage:
Monday: Tarun, nine, said Nanaji's story about the moon was wrong; his science book said otherwise. Mama snapped, "Respect your elders." Tarun went quiet, confused.
Thursday: He asked why he couldn't play at the park. "Don't argue. Respect your elders," said Mama again. Tarun muttered, "What does that even mean?" and got sent to his room.
Sunday: Indu masi, visiting, found him sulking. "Respect isn't being scared," she said. "It's being polite and caring. You can say, 'Nanaji, my book says something different, can I show you?' Gently." Tarun tried it at dinner. Nanaji put on his glasses, read the page and laughed. "Your book is cleverer than me." Tarun grinned.

qa.q: What did Nanaji say after reading the page?
qa.a: "Your book is cleverer than me."

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when he was told "Respect your elders" again on Thursday?
qa.a: He felt confused and frustrated, not understanding what it meant, and muttered back.

qa.q: How did Indu masi help Tarun?
qa.a: She explained that respect means politeness and care, not fear, and gave him gentle words to disagree with, so he kept his manners and his voice.

qa.q: How might Nanaji have felt when Tarun asked politely?
qa.a: He probably felt amused and pleased, happy to be shown something rather than argued with.

grounding: It illustrates a child told to respect elders without reasons, and an adult who explains respect as courtesy and care, not fear.
